summary: Tata Consumer Products buys tea, coffee, salt and other foods, blends and packs them, and sells them as brands such as Tata Tea, Tata Salt, Tata Sampann, Tetley and Eight O’Clock in shops in India and abroad.
description: Most of the work is buying, blending, packing and getting goods onto shop shelves. Tata Consumer buys tea leaves at auctions or directly from growers, blends them and packs them as Tata Tea or Tetley. It packs iodised salt as Tata Salt, and dals, spices and dry fruits as Tata Sampann. It also sells bottled water, ready-to-drink glucose drinks, sauces and noodles, and coffee in the United States. It says its brands reach 290 million Indian households through 4.5 million shops. It also makes instant coffee for other companies and, with Starbucks, runs Starbucks cafés in India.
money: Tata Consumer earns by selling packed goods to distributors, supermarket chains and online stores, which resell them to shoppers. A smaller part comes from selling instant coffee and tea extracts to other companies and from coffee grown on its own estates. Its main costs are tea, coffee and other raw materials, packaging, advertising, transport and staff. The price paid by a distributor is revenue, not profit.
customers: Households are the final buyers of a packet of tea or salt, but Tata Consumer is mostly paid by dealers who distribute to retailers, by supermarket chains and by online and quick-delivery apps. Abroad, supermarkets buy Tetley and Eight O’Clock. Other food and drink companies buy its instant coffee. Café visitors pay Tata Starbucks, a separate joint company.
drivers: How many packets it sells, especially of tea and salt, the cost of tea and coffee compared with the prices it can charge, and whether newer brands such as Tata Sampann and ready-to-drink beverages keep growing.

groups.title: Tea and coffee in India
groups.examples: Tata Tea Premium, Tata Tea Gold, Tetley green tea, Tata Coffee Grand and Sonnets coffee.
groups.explanation: Packed tea and coffee for homes. Tata Consumer says it owns India’s second-largest tea brand. Tea is a crop bought at auctions, so its cost moves with weather and harvests.

groups.title: Salt and pantry foods
groups.examples: Tata Salt, Tata Salt Lite, Tata Sampann dals, spices and dry fruits, and Tata Soulfull millet foods.
groups.explanation: Everyday kitchen staples. Tata Salt is India’s largest salt brand. Tata Sampann sells unpolished dals, spices, dry fruits and cold-pressed oils.

groups.title: Drinks and ready foods
groups.examples: Himalayan mineral water, Tata Gluco Plus, Tata Copper Plus water, Ching’s Secret sauces and noodles, and Smith & Jones cooking pastes.
groups.explanation: Products bought on the go or for quick cooking. Tata Consumer groups these with Tata Sampann and Organic India as its growth businesses.

groups.title: Brands sold abroad
groups.examples: Tetley tea bags in the UK and Canada, Eight O’Clock coffee in the United States, and Good Earth and Teapigs teas.
groups.explanation: Packed tea and coffee sold in foreign supermarkets. Tetley joined the company in 2000. These sales are earned in pounds, dollars and other currencies.

groups.title: Business sales and cafés
groups.examples: Instant coffee and tea extracts sold to other companies, coffee from its own estates, and Starbucks cafés in India.
groups.explanation: The instant coffee and estate business is reported as non-branded. Tata Starbucks is a joint company; its café sales are not in Tata Consumer’s revenue.

basics.title: What is a branded consumer goods company?
basics.text: It sells everyday items, like tea and salt, under a name shoppers recognise and buy again and again. It earns more than an unbranded seller because people trust the brand, but it must keep spending on advertising and on getting its packs into shops.

basics.title: Who stands between the factory and the shopper?
basics.text: Dealers, also called distributors, buy goods from the company and deliver them to small shops. Supermarket chains and online and quick-delivery apps buy directly. The company is paid when it sells to these sellers, not when the household buys.

basics.title: What is underlying volume growth?
basics.text: Underlying volume growth (UVG) measures how much more product, by quantity, the company sold than a year earlier. It separates selling more packets from simply charging more per packet.

steps.title: Buy the raw materials
steps.text: Tata Consumer buys tea at public auctions or by private deals, and buys coffee, pulses, spices and other ingredients. Prices change with weather and harvests.

steps.title: Blend, process and pack
steps.text: The tea is blended to a steady taste, salt and dals are cleaned and packed, and everything is sealed in branded packs.

steps.title: Sell to distributors and stores
steps.text: Packs go to dealers, supermarket chains and online stores, which pay Tata Consumer under agreed terms. This sale is its revenue.

steps.title: Advertise to bring shoppers back
steps.text: The company spends on advertising and promotions so that shoppers ask for its brands. In India this was about 5.5% of sales in July to September 2026.

steps.title: Shoppers buy and the cycle repeats
steps.text: Households buy from the shop, and the shop reorders from the distributor. Revenue (what sellers are billed), profit (what is left after all costs) and cash collected are different things.

specifics.title: Tea costs move with the weather
specifics.text: Tea is sold at auction and its price changes with harvests. Tata Consumer adjusts its prices in steps; when tea costs eased in 2025–26, it says it passed the benefit on to shoppers.

specifics.title: New brands are a growing share
specifics.text: Tata Sampann, ready-to-drink drinks, Tata Soulfull, Capital Foods and Organic India together made up 38% of the India business in July to September 2026, up from 8% in 2020–21.

specifics.title: Three ways of selling, three kinds of risk
specifics.text: The company reports India branded, international branded and non-branded businesses separately. Each has different customers, currencies and raw material risks.

specifics.title: Online and quick delivery are growing fast
specifics.text: In India, online shopping including quick-delivery apps contributed 19% of revenue in 2025–26, the company says, while traditional neighbourhood shops remain the backbone of its selling.

watch: Is Indian tea selling more packets again?
Tea is one of the biggest Indian businesses, and volumes were flat in July to September 2026.
Compare tea volume and revenue growth in each quarterly presentation and read the comments on price changes.
Are tea and coffee costs rising or falling?
Raw material cost is a large part of each packet, and price changes reach shoppers with a delay.
Read the annual report’s commodity risk section and the quarterly comments on tea and coffee prices, then compare with profit margin.
Are the growth businesses making money, not only sales?
New brands need advertising and distribution spending before they earn steady profits.
Follow the growth businesses’ share of India revenue each quarter and look for comments on their margins in the annual report.
How exposed is it to the pound and the dollar?
International sales are earned in foreign currencies, so a stronger rupee lowers their value in rupees.
Compare international revenue growth with and without currency changes, which the company reports as constant-currency growth.
Café sales are outside revenue, so only Tata Consumer’s share of profit or loss reaches its results.
Find the share of profit from joint ventures in the consolidated results and the Tata Starbucks section of the annual report.
risks: Tea is a crop sold at auction whose supply can change quickly with the weather, and coffee prices are also volatile. Higher costs squeeze profit until prices are raised.
Sales in the UK, United States, Canada and Australia are earned in foreign currencies, so exchange-rate changes alter their value in rupees.
India tea volumes were flat in July to September 2026 amid subdued demand, and the UK tea market was hit by a heatwave.
Exports from Capital Foods and Organic India were held back by shipping disruption in July to September 2026, slowing their growth.
Quick-delivery apps are growing fast. Tata Consumer has to keep investing to stay visible both online and in traditional shops.
context: July to September 2026: salt up, tea flat

On 26 October 2026 Tata Consumer said revenue rose 14% from a year earlier, with India volumes up 11%. Salt revenue grew 15%, while India tea volumes were flat amid subdued demand. Its growth businesses grew 40% and reached 38% of the India business. Tata Starbucks ended the quarter with 505 cafés in 81 cities. This describes one quarter.

financialNotes.title: Separate the brands, the business sales and the cafés
financialNotes.text: Tata Consumer’s consolidated results include India branded, international branded and non-branded businesses as separate segments. Tata Starbucks is a joint venture, so its café sales are outside revenue. stepsTitle: From a tea auction to a kitchen shelf.

quick.title: What it does
quick.text: Tata Consumer buys tea, coffee, salt and other foods, packs them under its brands and sells them in India and abroad, mainly through shops.

quick.title: Who pays
quick.text: Distributors, supermarket chains and online stores pay Tata Consumer and resell to households. Abroad, supermarkets buy its tea and coffee, and other companies buy its instant coffee.

quick.title: How it earns
quick.text: From selling packed food and drinks. Tea and salt are the biggest Indian products. A smaller part comes from instant coffee and coffee estates.

quick.title: What it spends on
quick.text: Tea leaves, coffee and other raw materials, packaging, advertising, transport to shops and staff.

helps.title: Brands people already buy
helps.text: Tata Consumer says Tata Salt is India’s largest salt brand and Tata Tea the second-largest tea brand, and that it is the world’s second-largest branded tea company. Familiar brands make repeat buying more likely.

helps.title: Very wide reach
helps.text: It says its products reach 290 million Indian households through 4.5 million shops, so a new product can be placed on many shelves quickly.

helps.title: Newer brands growing fast
helps.text: Tata Sampann revenue grew 57% and ready-to-drink revenue 47% in July to September 2026, adding growth beyond tea and salt.

hurts.title: Tea, the oldest business, is flat
hurts.text: India tea volumes did not grow in July to September 2026, and revenue was slightly lower than a year earlier.

hurts.title: Coffee estate income fell
hurts.text: Lower Vietnamese coffee prices reduced what its plantations business earned in July to September 2026.

hurts.title: Overseas tea was hit by weather
hurts.text: In the UK, a long heatwave cut tea drinking in July to September 2026, and international revenue fell 2% once currency movements are taken out.
